result.output:
{"body":"## Problem

On the Results view's **Pipeline runs** tab, the "Failure reason" column (`frontend/src/pages/Results.tsx`, the `columns: ColumnsType<PipelineRun>` array around the `failure_reason` entry) has no `width` and no `ellipsis`. `pipeline_runs.failure_reason` is `String(2048)` on the backend (`backend/app/db/models.py`) — a real provider error string (ADF/Airflow) can be very long. With no bound, a long value stretches the whole column (and the table's horizontal scrollbar with it) to fit the entire string on one line, making the scrollbar unusably long and the table hard to use.

## Fix

Give the column a bounded fixed width with single-line ellipsis, and reveal the full text on hover — the standard antd pattern: `width: <px>` + `ellipsis: { showTitle: false }` on the column, with the cell's `render` wrapped in a `<Tooltip title={fullText}>` (custom tooltip since `showTitle: false` suppresses antd's own native-title one). Keep the existing `'—'` null placeholder un-tooltipped.

## Scope

1. Primary: the pipeline-runs "Failure reason" column.
2. Audit every other antd `Table` (`ColumnsType` definitions) across `frontend/src` for columns rendering unbounded free text (error/reason/message/description-like content) and apply the same treatment where warranted. Columns that are already bounded (tags, timestamps, fixed-vocabulary status, names capped at input) are out of scope.","comments":[{"id":"IC_kwDOSBITx88AAAABN2yAJw","author":{"login":"TheurgicDuke771"},"authorAssociation":"OWNER","body":"Audit result (full detail in PR #1185's description, "Audit — tables inspected"): the only other candidate for this bug class found across every `ColumnsType` table in `frontend/src` was `RunDetail.tsx`'s "Observed" column (`observed_value`, rendered via `ScalarValue`/`formatScalar`, which can `JSON.stringify` an object).

Determination: **verified-benign, scoped out of this fix.** Traced the GX translation path (`backend/app/datasources/gx_runner.py`, `monitors.py`) — for every check kind DataQ ships (expectation aggregates, freshness/volume/anomaly/comparison), `observed_value` is a compact scalar/small dict (counts, percentages, a timestamp); the actual unexpected-value lists live in `sample_failures`/`partial_unexpected_list`, which this column doesn't render. JSON output also has natural wrap points (commas/brackets), unlike the single unbroken provider-error string that caused this issue. It's also the row's primary "answer," so truncating it behind a hover is a worse tradeoff than for a secondary "reason" column.

No follow-up issue filed — recording the determination here per the fixed-or-filed rule so it isn't dropped silently. If a real-world `observed_value` payload is ever found to actually stretch the table, re-open or file fresh against that evidence.","createdAt":"2026-08-08T05:57:57Z","includesCreatedEdit":false,"isMinimized":false,"minimizedReason":"","reactionGroups":[],"url":"https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1184#issuecomment-5224824871","viewerDidAuthor":true},{"id":"IC_kwDOSBITx88AAAABN4he8A","author":{"login":"TheurgicDuke771"},"authorAssociation":"OWNER","body":"**Correction to the "verified-benign" determination above.**

A live user report against the run-detail page's Observed column contradicted the "always a compact scalar/small dict" premise, so it was re-investigated (#1207).

The premise holds for `anomaly` and for GX/custom-SQL expectations (incl. #1201's UC custom-SQL fix) — both genuinely store a fixed small scalar shape in `observed_value`. It does **not** hold for `schema_drift` (`added`/`removed` column-name lists + a `type_changed` list, one entry per drifted column) or `comparison` (ADR 0015 — `per_column`/`column_mismatch_counts` dicts keyed by every compared column). Both scale with column count, not a fixed shape, and the original audit (tracing `gx_runner.py`/`monitors.py`) didn't reach the two monitor-kind services (`schema_drift.py`, `comparison_run.py`) that build `observed_value` themselves outside the shared GX runner.

Fixed in #1207 (bounded width + tooltip on the Observed column, same pattern as this issue's fix). Recording the correction here per the working agreement — determinations get corrected on the record, never silently.

1	# Local DataQ ⟷ prod mirror — session summary + runbook
2	
3	**Session: 2026-08-03.** DataQ's local dev stack was converted into a live
4	mirror of prod (real secrets, real connections/suites, real datasource
5	traffic) and the local harness stack (this repo's `local/`) was brought up
6	alongside it. This doc is the replication runbook for redoing that, plus
7	guidance on using the mirror day-to-day and on actually exercising the local
8	Airflow/MinIO stack (which, as of this session, sits up but **unused** — see
9	§4).
10	
11	Companion: DataQ's own memory note
12	`~/.claude/projects/-Users-arijit-Coding-Python-DataQ/memory/project_local_prod_mirror_setup.md`
13	carries the same gotchas for AI-assistant sessions; this file is the
14	human-readable, repo-anchored version.
15	
16	---
17	
18	## 1. What was done this session
19	
20	1. **Brought up DataQ's own compose stack** (`docker compose up -d` in
21	   `~/Coding/Python/DataQ`) — postgres/redis/openbao/mailpit/api/worker/frontend,
22	   all default services.
23	2. **Brought up this repo's local harness** (`local/harness_local.sh up`) —
24	   Airflow (Postgres+Redis+CeleryExecutor) + MinIO, joined onto DataQ's
25	   compose network.
26	3. **Configured multi-user email-OTP sign-in** by setting `DATAQ_SIGNIN_EMAIL`
27	   in DataQ's root `.env` — see the gotcha in §2.2, this is the ONE switch,
28	   not a separately-settable allowlist.
29	4. **Mirrored local OpenBao onto Azure Key Vault exactly** — purged 143
30	   unrelated stale secrets from a prior local session, wrote in the 25 real
31	   `dataq-app-kv-aw6laj` secrets by name (values piped directly between `az`
32	   and OpenBao's HTTP API, never printed or written to disk), verified the
33	   name sets are now identical.
34	5. **Replaced local DB seed/demo data with prod's real `users` /
35	   `connections` / `suites` / `checks`** — nuked the local schema, re-ran
36	   migrations, opened a **temporary** Postgres firewall rule, copied the four
37	   tables straight from prod via `psycopg2`, closed the firewall rule
38	   immediately after. 13 connections, 12 suites, 30 checks, 8 users.
39	6. **Verified functionality**: OTP sign-in end-to-end (Mailpit), suite runs
40	   across Snowflake / ADLS flat-file / Unity Catalog (all green, including a
41	   deliberately-seeded prod failure behaving as expected) / Iceberg (failed —
42	   see §2.5, expected given the closed firewall rule).
43	7. **Backfilled asset resolution** — the raw DB copy bypassed the service
44	   layer that normally creates an `assets` row on suite save, so `GET
45	   /assets` was empty. Fixed by re-`PATCH`ing each suite with its own
46	   existing `target`, which forces `resolve_and_upsert_asset` without
47	   changing anything else. 10 assets now exist, correctly deduplicated.
48	8. **Reset a latent lineage-sync landmine** — the copied Unity Catalog
49	   connections carried prod's *incremental* lineage watermark
50	   (`2026-07-27`) into a local DB whose `lineage_edges` table was never
51	   copied. Left alone, a future local warehouse-lineage refresh would have
52	   silently started from that stale cursor and permanently skipped
53	   everything before it. Reset `lineage_watermark` /
54	   `lineage_last_refresh_at` / `lineage_last_tier` to `NULL` on both UC
55	   connections.
56	
57	**Not done (deliberately out of scope):** `trigger_bindings` / `schedules` /
58	`suite_notifications` / access-grants were not copied from prod — local
59	suites won't auto-fire on a cron or an orchestration trigger. Lineage edges
60	themselves were not copied and are not backfilled (they only populate via a
61	live refresh, which is off locally by default — same as prod).
62	
63	---
64	
65	## 2. Replication runbook (redo this from scratch)
66	
67	Run this in `~/Coding/Python/DataQ` unless noted. Requires `az` logged in
68	with Key Vault read + Container App secret read + the shared Postgres
69	server's firewall-rule permissions (deployer/`dataq-admin`-tier access).
70	
71	### 2.1 Bring up both stacks
72	
73	```bash
74	cd ~/Coding/Python/DataQ
75	docker compose up -d                       # postgres/redis/openbao/mailpit/api/worker/frontend
76	
77	cd ~/Coding/Python/DataQ-harness/local
78	./harness_local.sh up                      # requires DataQ's stack up first (joins dataq_default)
79	```
80	
81	### 2.2 Multi-user OTP sign-in
82	
83	`.env`'s `DATAQ_SIGNIN_EMAIL` **is** the allowlist — `docker-compose.yml`
84	wires it straight into `AUTH_OTP_ALLOWED_EMAILS` verbatim
85	(`${DATAQ_SIGNIN_EMAIL?...}`, not a separate override). Comma-separate it for
86	multiple users:
87	
88	```bash
89	# .env is deliberately unwritable by the Edit tool in an AI session (secrets
90	# guard) — append with a shell redirect instead:
91	printf 'DATAQ_SIGNIN_EMAIL=you@example.com,teammate@example.com\n' >> .env
92	docker compose up -d api worker             # env is a start-time snapshot
93	```
94	
95	`WORKSPACE_ADMIN_EMAILS` defaults to `dev-bypass@dataq.local,${DATAQ_SIGNIN_EMAIL}`
96	— so every signed-in address is workspace-admin by default, which is what
97	gives a freshly-provisioned local user visibility into prod's suites (they
98	belong to prod's *user rows*, not to whichever new email you sign in with;
99	workspace-admin has implicit visibility into everything, ADR 0027).
100	
101	### 2.3 Mirror OpenBao onto Key Vault (exact set, no extras)
102	
103	```bash
104	KV=dataq-app-kv-aw6laj   # re-verify with `az keyvault list` in case it's been renamed
105	source .env.app          # OPENBAO_ADDR / OPENBAO_MOUNT / OPENBAO_TOKEN
106	
107	az keyvault secret list --vault-name "$KV" --query "[?attributes.enabled].name" -o tsv | sort > /tmp/kv_names.txt
108	
109	curl -s -H "X-Vault-Token: $OPENBAO_TOKEN" "$OPENBAO_ADDR/v1/$OPENBAO_MOUNT/metadata?list=true" \
110	  | python3 -c "import json,sys; print('\n'.join(sorted(json.load(sys.stdin)['data']['keys'])))" > /tmp/local_names.txt
111	
112	# purge anything local-only
113	comm -23 /tmp/local_names.txt /tmp/kv_names.txt | while read -r n; do
114	  curl -s -o /dev/null -X DELETE -H "X-Vault-Token: $OPENBAO_TOKEN" "$OPENBAO_ADDR/v1/$OPENBAO_MOUNT/metadata/$n"
115	done
116	
117	# write in every KV secret (value piped straight through, never echoed/printed)
118	while read -r n; do
119	  az keyvault secret show --vault-name "$KV" --name "$n" --query value -o tsv \
120	    | python3 -c "import sys,json; print(json.dumps({'data':{'value': sys.stdin.readline().rstrip(chr(10))}}))" \
121	    | curl -s -o /dev/null -X POST -H "X-Vault-Token: $OPENBAO_TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
122	      --data-binary @- "$OPENBAO_ADDR/v1/$OPENBAO_MOUNT/data/$n"
123	done < /tmp/kv_names.txt
124	```
125	
126	**Gotcha:** this purge also deletes `dataq-local-smtp` — the bundled Mailpit
127	catcher's password, seeded locally by the one-shot `otp-mail-secret` compose
128	service. It never exists in prod Key Vault by design (prod mails via Gmail
129	SMTP under different secret names), so a strict "match KV exactly" diff
130	always removes it, and OTP sign-in then fails with
131	`otp_email_not_configured`. Fix, every time:
132	
133	```bash
134	docker compose up -d --force-recreate otp-mail-secret
135	```
136	
137	### 2.4 Wipe local seed data, pull in prod's real data
138	
139	```bash
140	cd ~/Coding/Python/DataQ
141	
142	# 1. temp access to the shared prod Postgres server
143	MYIP=$(curl -s https://api.ipify.org)
144	az postgres flexible-server firewall-rule create -g dataq-rg --server-name dataq-pg-wus3-3erlgd \
145	  --name "temp-local-sync-$(python3 -c 'import time;print(int(time.time()))')" \
146	  --start-ip-address "$MYIP" --end-ip-address "$MYIP"
147	
148	# 2. resolve prod's DATABASE_URL — it is NOT in any tfvars file (apply-time-only var);
149	#    read it straight off the live Container App secret instead:
150	export PROD_DATABASE_URL=$(az containerapp secret list -n dataq-app-api -g dataq-rg --show-values -o json \
151	  | python3 -c "import json,sys; d=json.load(sys.stdin); print(next(s['value'] for s in d if s['name']=='database-url'))")
152	
153	# 3. nuke local schema, re-migrate (NO reseed — that's exactly the demo data being removed)
154	docker compose exec -T postgres psql -U dataq -d dataq -c "DROP SCHEMA public CASCADE; CREATE SCHEMA public;"
155	export LOCAL_DATABASE_URL="REDACTED"
156	(cd backend && DATABASE_URL="$LOCAL_DATABASE_URL" conda run -n dataq alembic upgrade head)
157	# Gotcha: `conda run -n dataq sh -c "cd backend && alembic upgrade head"` alone fails with
158	# "no password supplied" — pydantic-settings' env_file=".env.app" resolves relative to cwd,
159	# and there is no backend/.env.app (only the repo-root one). Export DATABASE_URL explicitly.
160	
161	# 4. copy users -> connections -> suites -> checks, in that FK order
162	conda run -n dataq python /path/to/sync_prod_data.py   # script below
163	
164	# 5. close the firewall rule immediately
165	RULE=$(az postgres flexible-server firewall-rule list -g dataq-rg --server-name dataq-pg-wus3-3erlgd \
166	  --query "[?starts_with(name,'temp-local-sync-')].name" -o tsv)
167	az postgres flexible-server firewall-rule delete -g dataq-rg --server-name dataq-pg-wus3-3erlgd --name "$RULE" --yes
168	```
169	
170	`sync_prod_data.py` (generic reflection-based copy, JSONB-safe, nulls
171	`asset_id` since `assets` is out of scope):
172	
173	```python
174	import os, sys
175	import psycopg2
176	import psycopg2.extras
177	
178	PROD_URL = os.environ["PROD_DATABASE_URL"].replace("postgresql+psycopg2://", "postgresql://")
179	LOCAL_URL = os.environ["LOCAL_DATABASE_URL"].replace("postgresql+psycopg2://", "postgresql://")
180	TABLES = ["users", "connections", "suites", "checks"]   # FK order
181	
182	prod = psycopg2.connect(PROD_URL); prod.set_session(readonly=True, autocommit=True)
183	local = psycopg2.connect(LOCAL_URL); local.autocommit = False
184	
185	try:
186	    with local.cursor() as lcur:
187	        for table in TABLES:
188	            with prod.cursor(cursor_factory=psycopg2.extras.RealDictCursor) as pcur:
189	                pcur.execute(f"SELECT * FROM {table}")
190	                rows = pcur.fetchall()
191	            if not rows:
192	                print(f"{table}: 0 rows, skipping"); continue
193	            cols = list(rows[0].keys())
194	            if "asset_id" in cols:
195	                for r in rows: r["asset_id"] = None
196	            for r in rows:
197	                for k, v in r.items():
198	                    if isinstance(v, (dict, list)):
199	                        r[k] = psycopg2.extras.Json(v)
200	            col_list = ", ".join(f'"{c}"' for c in cols)
201	            placeholders = ", ".join(f"%({c})s" for c in cols)
202	            psycopg2.extras.execute_batch(
203	                lcur, f'INSERT INTO {table} ({col_list}) VALUES ({placeholders})', rows
204	            )
205	            print(f"{table}: inserted {len(rows)} rows")
206	    local.commit(); print("COMMIT ok")
207	except Exception:
208	    local.rollback(); raise
209	finally:
210	    prod.close(); local.close()
211	```
212	
213	### 2.5 Backfill assets + fix the lineage watermark (after the copy, every time)
214	
215	The copy above bypasses `suite_service`, so `assets` stays empty until you
216	force a resolve. For every suite, `PATCH` it with its **own current**
217	`target` (fetch via `GET /suites`, resend the same `target` dict — `None`
218	means "unchanged" in this API, so you must resend it explicitly to trigger
219	resolution):
220	
221	```bash
222	curl -s -b cookies.txt -X PATCH "http://localhost:8000/api/v1/suites/$SUITE_ID" \
223	  -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d "{\"target\": $TARGET_JSON}"
224	```
225	
226	Then reset the UC lineage watermark so a future warehouse-lineage refresh
227	doesn't silently skip history it never actually has locally:
228	
229	```bash
230	docker compose exec -T postgres psql -U dataq -d dataq -c \
231	  "UPDATE connections SET lineage_watermark = NULL, lineage_last_refresh_at = NULL, lineage_last_tier = NULL WHERE type = 'unity_catalog';"
232	```
233	
234	(Snowflake connections don't need this — their lineage pull is a full
235	snapshot re-read each time, not incremental.)
236	
237	---
238	
239	## 3. Using this mirror for local testing
240	
241	Once §2 is done, the local stack behaves like a real, working copy of prod:
242	
243	- **Sign in** at `http://localhost:3000` (or via the OTP API directly:
244	  `POST /api/v1/auth/otp/request` → read the code at
245	  `http://localhost:8025` → `POST /api/v1/auth/otp/verify`).
246	- **All 13 real connections and 12 real suites** are there, pointed at the
247	  actual live Snowflake/ADLS/UC/ADF/Airflow/dbt/Iceberg endpoints — a suite
248	  run genuinely queries the live warehouse, same as it would in prod. Trigger
249	  one with `POST /suites/{id}/run`, poll `GET /runs/{id}`.
250	- **Connection tests** (`POST /connections/{id}/test`) are a fast, read-only
251	  way to confirm the OpenBao mirror is intact without running a full suite.
252	- **Assets/lineage**: the asset view (`GET /assets/{id}`) works normally —
253	  scorecard, dimension coverage, linked suites. Lineage edges stay empty
254	  unless you flip `WAREHOUSE_LINEAGE_ENABLED=true` in `.env.app` and either
255	  wait for the daily `02:37 UTC` beat task or trigger
256	  `refresh_warehouse_lineage` manually via a Celery call.
257	- **What won't work**: cron schedules and orchestration triggers, since
258	  `schedules`/`trigger_bindings` weren't copied (§1). A suite will only run
259	  when you trigger it manually.
260	- **Re-syncing later**: OpenBao is **dev-mode / in-memory** — it loses
261	  everything on `docker compose down` or a container restart. Re-run §2.3
262	  after any restart. The DB copy in §2.4 is durable (real Postgres volume)
263	  until you next reset it.
264	
265	---
266	
267	## 4. Utilizing the local Airflow + MinIO stack
268	
269	**As of this session, they are up but genuinely unused** — none of the 13
270	prod-mirrored connections point at them (they all point at the real Azure
271	endpoints, matching prod). MinIO's `landing` bucket and the Airflow scheduler
272	still hold state from an **older** session (mockdata seeded 2026-07-27; DAG
273	runs `flow_a_snowflake_load` / `flow_a_uc_reference` / `flow_b_medallion`
274	last shown `failed` from that same old run) — nothing from the 2026-08-03
275	session touched them.
276	
277	To actually exercise them, two independent things need to happen:
278	
279	**A. Re-seed / re-run the harness itself** (tests the ETL flow in isolation,
280	nothing to do with DataQ yet):
281	
282	```bash
283	cd ~/Coding/Python/DataQ-harness/local
284	./harness_local.sh seed          # backfill mockdata -> MinIO
285	./harness_local.sh run --dags    # unpause + REST-trigger the cron DAGs
286	./harness_local.sh status        # container + DAG state
287	```
288	
289	Airflow UI: `http://localhost:8080` (admin / see `local/.env`). MinIO
290	console: `http://localhost:9001`.
291	
292	**B. Point a DataQ connection at them** (this is what actually puts them in
293	DataQ's monitoring path — see the harness README's "Point DataQ at it"
294	section for the full detail, summarized here):
295	
296	- **MinIO as an `s3` connection** (DataQ #1063, ordinary `s3` connection
297	  type, no special local mode): `bucket=landing`, `region=us-east-1`,
298	  `endpoint_url=http://minio:9000`, access key/secret =
299	  `MINIO_ROOT_USER`/`MINIO_ROOT_PASSWORD` (from `local/.env`). Leave
300	  addressing style `auto` — it resolves to **path** style automatically
301	  because an endpoint is set (MinIO only serves the bucket in the path).
302	- **Local Airflow as an `airflow` connection**: `base_url=http://airflow-webserver:8080`,
303	  basic auth, user `admin`, password from `local/.env`.
304	
305	Either create these as **new, additional** local-only connections/suites (so
306	you don't disturb the prod-mirrored ones), or temporarily repoint one of the
307	mirrored flat-file/orchestration connections at the local endpoints if you
308	specifically want to compare local vs. prod behavior on the same suite
309	definition.
310	
311	This combination (§4A + §4B) was **validated end-to-end once already**, on
312	2026-07-27, before this session (see DataQ's `docs/ops-log.md`): 4 DAGs
313	parsed clean, 24 datasets seeded, DataQ connection test green, flat-file
314	suite 4/4 (643 rows, arrival-time freshness read off MinIO's
315	`LastModified`), `flow_a_snowflake_load` succeeded into live Snowflake, and
316	DataQ ingested the local DAG runs into `pipeline_runs`. That state is what's
317	currently sitting stale in the containers — re-running §4A brings it current
318	again; §4B (the DataQ-side connection) was not re-created this session and
319	would need to be added again if you want DataQ itself watching the local
320	harness rather than just the harness running standalone.
321	
322	---
323	
324	## 5. Teardown
325	
326	```bash
327	# local harness
328	cd ~/Coding/Python/DataQ-harness/local
329	./harness_local.sh down            # add --volumes to also drop the metadata DB + MinIO data
330	
331	# DataQ stack
332	cd ~/Coding/Python/DataQ
333	docker compose down                 # add -v to also drop Postgres/OpenBao data
334	```
335	
336	Nothing here touches Azure/prod — every prod-facing action in §2 is either
337	read-only (`az keyvault secret show`, the prod `SELECT`s) or explicitly
338	scoped and reverted (the firewall rule).

"""Flow D — Apache Iceberg writer (no orchestrator).

Each ``iceberg-tick`` appends a referentially-consistent batch of purchase-order
rows to the Iceberg table ``retail.purchase_orders`` via a pyiceberg **SqlCatalog**
(Postgres-backed metadata) with an **ADLS (abfss) warehouse** read through
fsspec/adlfs. DataQ reads the same table **natively** (its ``iceberg`` connection,
ADR 0030) on its own DataQ schedule — there is **no orchestrator and no
trigger-binding** (the Flow-C precedent: nothing "loads" this for DataQ to react to).

Self-contained by design — unlike the ``tick`` feeds this needs **no persisted
state file**. Each tick simply appends another snapshot (idempotent-safe: re-running
just adds another batch). ``po_id`` is namespaced by the tick's wall-clock so two
ticks never collide (which would forge an *accidental* duplicate and muddy the one
*deliberate* duplicate we seed). Supplier / product ids come from the same seeded
pools idiom (``rng.id_pool``) the rest of the harness uses, so they read as the same
id space as Flow A's ``suppliers`` / ``products``.

Seeded DQ issues per tick (mirrors ``dq_issues.py`` rates/style) give DataQ's checks
something real to bite on: ~1-2% negative ``order_qty`` (fails a ``order_qty >= 0``
range check), ~1% null ``supplier_id`` (fails ``not_null supplier_id``), and a rare
duplicate ``(po_id, po_line)`` (fails a uniqueness check).

The pyiceberg / pyarrow imports are module-local to the functions that need a live
catalog so ``python -m mockdata --help`` (and the other subcommands) don't pay for
them; ``iceberg-tick`` is the only path that requires the Iceberg deps.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import datetime as dt
import os
from typing import Any

from .rng import Rng

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Table coordinates + generation shape.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

NAMESPACE = "retail"
TABLE = "purchase_orders"
IDENTIFIER = f"{NAMESPACE}.{TABLE}"

# Referential pools (same id shapes as Flow A: SUP-#### width 4, SKU-###### width 6).
N_SUPPLIERS = 30
N_PRODUCTS = 200

# Batch sizing + issue rates (mirror dq_issues.py: low single-digit %).
DEFAULT_ROWS_MIN = 200
DEFAULT_ROWS_MAX = 500
NEG_QTY_RATE = 0.015  # ~1.5% negative order_qty
NULL_SUPPLIER_RATE = 0.01  # ~1% null supplier_id
DUP_RATE = 0.005  # ~0.5% duplicated (po_id, po_line) rows

PO_STATUSES = ["open", "partial", "received", "cancelled"]
CURRENCIES = ["USD", "EUR", "GBP", "CAD", "JPY"]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Catalog wiring.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def catalog_properties_from_env() -> dict[str, str]:
    """Compose ``load_catalog`` / ``SqlCatalog`` properties from the Job's env.

    ``ICEBERG_CATALOG_URI`` (the Postgres SQLAlchemy DSN, secret) + ``ICEBERG_WAREHOUSE``
    (the ``abfss://iceberg@<acct>.dfs.core.windows.net/warehouse`` root) + the ADLS
    account name/key for the fsspec (adlfs) FileIO. Mirrors the DataQ ``iceberg``
    connection's own catalog properties (``IcebergConfig.catalog_properties``) so both
    sides read the same table the same way.
    """
    uri = os.environ["ICEBERG_CATALOG_URI"]
    warehouse = os.environ["ICEBERG_WAREHOUSE"]
    props: dict[str, str] = {
        "uri": uri,
        "warehouse": warehouse,
        # Native (no query engine) object-store IO through fsspec/adlfs.
        "py-io-impl": "pyiceberg.io.fsspec.FsspecFileIO",
    }

def build_catalog(
    name: str = "harness", *, properties: dict[str, str] | None = None
) -> Any:
    """Load a pyiceberg ``SqlCatalog`` (env-driven by default).

    ``properties`` overrides the env composition — the local sqlite smoke passes a
    ``sqlite://`` uri + a ``file://`` warehouse so the writer's real code paths run
    with no Azure. pyiceberg is imported here so the CLI stays import-cheap.
    """
    from pyiceberg.catalog.sql import SqlCatalog

    props = properties if properties is not None else catalog_properties_from_env()
    return SqlCatalog(name, **props)


def _iceberg_schema() -> Any:
    """The ``retail.purchase_orders`` Iceberg schema (v2).

    ``po_id`` / ``po_line`` / ``load_ts`` are required (the batch always populates
    them); everything else is **optional** so the seeded null ``supplier_id`` lands
    instead of being rejected at write time. ``unit_cost`` is a ``double`` — it
    round-trips through pyarrow cleanly, avoiding decimal128 scale/precision friction
    on ``table.append`` (the design's allowed choice).
    """
    from pyiceberg.schema import Schema
    from pyiceberg.types import (
        DateType,
        DoubleType,
        IntegerType,
        NestedField,
        StringType,
        TimestamptzType,
    )

    return Schema(
        NestedField(1, "po_id", StringType(), required=True),
        NestedField(2, "po_line", IntegerType(), required=True),
        NestedField(3, "supplier_id", StringType(), required=False),
        NestedField(4, "product_id", StringType(), required=False),
        NestedField(5, "order_qty", IntegerType(), required=False),
        NestedField(6, "unit_cost", DoubleType(), required=False),
        NestedField(7, "currency", StringType(), required=False),
        NestedField(8, "status", StringType(), required=False),
        NestedField(9, "ordered_at", TimestamptzType(), required=False),
        NestedField(10, "expected_delivery", DateType(), required=False),
        NestedField(11, "load_ts", TimestamptzType(), required=True),
    )


def _arrow_schema() -> Any:
    """pyarrow schema matching ``_iceberg_schema`` (nullability + widths aligned).

    IntegerType → int32; TimestamptzType → ``timestamp('us', tz='UTC')`` (pyiceberg's
    required microsecond precision); DateType → date32. Nullable flags mirror the
    Iceberg ``required`` flags so ``table.append`` accepts the frame."""
    import pyarrow as pa

    return pa.schema(
        [
            pa.field("po_id", pa.string(), nullable=False),
            pa.field("po_line", pa.int32(), nullable=False),
            pa.field("supplier_id", pa.string(), nullable=True),
            pa.field("product_id", pa.string(), nullable=True),
            pa.field("order_qty", pa.int32(), nullable=True),
            pa.field("unit_cost", pa.float64(), nullable=True),
            pa.field("currency", pa.string(), nullable=True),
            pa.field("status", pa.string(), nullable=True),
            pa.field("ordered_at", pa.timestamp("us", tz="UTC"), nullable=True),
            pa.field("expected_delivery", pa.date32(), nullable=True),
            pa.field("load_ts", pa.timestamp("us", tz="UTC"), nullable=False),
        ]

def ensure_table(catalog: Any) -> Any:
    """Create namespace + table if absent, then return the loaded table."""
    catalog.create_namespace_if_not_exists(NAMESPACE)
    return catalog.create_table_if_not_exists(IDENTIFIER, schema=_iceberg_schema())


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Batch generation.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def build_batch(rng: Rng, now: dt.datetime, rows: int) -> Any:
def run_tick(
    *,
    catalog: Any = None,
    properties: dict[str, str] | None = None,
    seed: int = 42,
    rows: int | None = None,
    now: dt.datetime | None = None,
) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Append one batch to ``retail.purchase_orders``; return commit stats.

    ``catalog`` (pre-built, used by the local smoke) takes precedence; otherwise a
    catalog is built from ``properties`` or the env. ``rows=None`` picks a seeded
    size in ``[DEFAULT_ROWS_MIN, DEFAULT_ROWS_MAX]``.
    """
    now = now or dt.datetime.now(dt.UTC)
    # Per-tick seed shift so successive ticks differ yet stay reproducible.
    tick_token = int(now.timestamp())
    rng = Rng(seed + tick_token)
    if rows is None:
        rows = rng.randint(DEFAULT_ROWS_MIN, DEFAULT_ROWS_MAX)

    cat = catalog if catalog is not None else build_catalog(properties=properties)
    table = ensure_table(cat)
    batch = build_batch(rng, now, rows)
    table.append(batch)

    table.refresh()
    snapshot = table.current_snapshot()
    snapshot_id = snapshot.snapshot_id if snapshot is not None else None
    total_rows = int(table.scan().count())

    print(
        f"iceberg-tick {IDENTIFIER}: appended {batch.num_rows} rows "
        f"snapshot_id={snapshot_id} total_table_rows={total_rows}"
    )
    return {
        "identifier": IDENTIFIER,
        "appended_rows": batch.num_rows,
        "snapshot_id": snapshot_id,
        "total_table_rows": total_rows,
    }

# DataQ Pre-Deploy QA Report — commit `1758cf8a` (local, 56 commits ahead of prod)

**Summary:** 2 new **blocker**-severity backend defects found (both first-time reproductions, neither matches an open GitHub issue); admin/non-admin flows, connection setup, and mobile rendering are otherwise healthy; #1208 confirmed fixed in source. **Go/no-go: NO-GO** until the Decimal-serialization bug is fixed — it can silently discard a real DQ failure on any Snowflake/UC suite.

---

## 1. Connection setup (Part 1) — all 4 created and tested successfully

| Datasource | Secret used | Test Connection | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Snowflake | `conn-snowflake-retail-dev-6729c4f9` (Password/PAT auth) | ✅ Connected | Auth type dropdown defaulted correctly to Password |
| Unity Catalog | `conn-unity-catalog-dataq-retail-dev-ae7b09b7` | ✅ Connected (first try, no fallback needed) | No `catalog` field on the connection form — catalog is set at suite-target level (`catalog.schema.table`), which is correct per the UC target model |
| AWS S3 (MinIO) | `MINIO_ROOT_USER`/`PASSWORD` from harness `.env` | ✅ Connected | `endpoint_url=http://minio:9000`, addressing left `auto` |
| Apache Iceberg | SQL catalog (`postgresql+psycopg2://dataq@postgres:5432/iceberg_catalog`, `catalog_name=harness`) + S3-override properties + storage secret + catalog DB password | ✅ Connected | **But see Finding #2 below — Test Connection does not catch the real failure mode.** |

## 2. Suite/run results per datasource (Part 2 + 3)

| Suite | Datasource | Target | PASS | FAIL | ERROR | schema_drift |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Snowflake Orders Header Suite | Snowflake | `RETAIL.ORDERS_HEADER` | ✅ pass | ✅ fail (`channel` not-in-set) | ✅ error (bad column ref, custom SQL) | ✅ pass, `baseline_captured: true` |
| UC Feedback Sentiment Suite | Unity Catalog | `dataq_retail.gold.feedback_sentiment` | ✅ pass | ✅ fail | ✅ error | — |
| S3 Orders Header CSV Suite | S3/MinIO | `snowflake/orders_header/orders_header.csv` | ✅ pass | ✅ fail | ✅ error (nonexistent column, clean message) | — |
| Iceberg Purchase Orders Suite | Iceberg | `retail.purchase_orders` | **blocked — see Finding #2** | | | |

All PASS/FAIL/ERROR states rendered correctly in the live-progress modal and the run-detail table, with correct severity tags and a clean, non-leaking ERROR message (e.g. `{"error":"(snowflake.connector.errors.ProgrammingError) 000904 (42000): ... invalid identifier 'NONEXISTENT_COLUMN_XYZ'"}` — bounded, no `[SQL: …] [parameters: …]` echo, confirming **#1203 stayed fixed**).

---

## 3. Findings

### Finding #1 — BLOCKER — FAIL results on a Snowflake/warehouse NUMERIC column crash the entire run, discarding all results

**Repro:** Snowflake suite, single check `expect_column_values_to_be_between` on `subtotal` (NUMERIC) with `min_value=1000000, max_value=2000000` (guaranteed 100% fail). Run status → `failed`, 0/1 checks persisted, no results at all — even though GX successfully computed the metric.

**Root cause (confirmed by direct reproduction inside the api container):**
```
TypeError: Object of type Decimal is not JSON serializable
```
in `sqlalchemy/sql/sqltypes.py` while bulk-inserting the `results` row's JSONB columns. `backend/app/core/jsonsafe.py:24` (`sanitize_json`) explicitly handles numpy scalars, pandas `NA`/`NaT`, dates, and non-finite floats — but has **no branch for `decimal.Decimal`**. When a range check *fails* on a warehouse NUMERIC column, GX's failing-sample/observed-value payload carries the raw `Decimal` values from that column (e.g. the actual `subtotal` amounts), which flow unsanitized into `observed_value`/`sample_failures` via `backend/app/services/run_service.py:113-118` (`_build_result`). A **passing** check on the same column never crashes (the empty failing-list has no Decimal to leak), which is exactly why this was easy to miss in earlier testing.

**Isolation proof (each run individually verified via worker logs):**
- `order_number not null` alone → succeeds (`n_results=1`)
- `subtotal` range **0–100000 (passes)** → succeeds
- `subtotal` range **1000000–2000000 (fails)** → crashes with the exact Decimal TypeError, reproduced twice independently (once inside the original 4-check batch, once alone)
- `channel` in-set FAIL (string column) → succeeds normally, confirming the bug is Decimal-specific, not FAIL-status-generic

**Impact:** Any Snowflake or Unity-Catalog suite with a range/threshold check on a currency, quantity, or other NUMERIC column that legitimately fails will silently lose the entire run's results — precisely the "the check actually caught something" scenario a DQ platform exists to preserve. Not matched by any open GitHub issue (`gh issue list` searched for "Decimal", empty). **This must block the prod deploy.**

**Fix direction:** add a `decimal.Decimal` branch to `sanitize_json` (e.g. `if isinstance(value, decimal.Decimal): return float(value)`), mirroring the existing numpy/pandas coercion pattern.

### Finding #2 — BLOCKER (scoped to Iceberg+S3-compatible storage) — pyiceberg's PyArrow S3 FileIO gets `ACCESS_DENIED` reading table metadata from MinIO; "Test Connection" doesn't catch it

**Repro:** Iceberg connection (Test Connection: ✅ Connected) → any column-listing call or check dry-run against `retail.purchase_orders` → 502 `profile_failed` / `dry_run_failed`.

**Root cause (confirmed by direct reproduction inside the api container, `load_iceberg_table` in `backend/app/datasources/iceberg.py:222-241`):**
```
OSError: When reading information for key 'warehouse/retail/purchase_orders/metadata/00006-....metadata.json'
in bucket 'iceberg': AWS Error ACCESS_DENIED during HeadObject operation: No response body.

  --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Problem

Any Snowflake or Unity Catalog check that legitimately **fails** on a NUMERIC/DECIMAL column (price, quantity, subtotal, etc.) crashes the entire run during results persistence:

```
TypeError: Object of type Decimal is not JSON serializable
```

The crash happens in the JSONB bulk-insert of the `results` row (`backend/app/services/run_service.py`, `_run_suite`'s bulk insert). `backend/app/core/jsonsafe.py`'s `sanitize_json` (line ~24) explicitly coerces numpy scalars, pandas `NA`/`NaT`, dates, and non-finite floats — but has **no branch for `decimal.Decimal`**.

**Why it's easy to miss:** a *passing* check on a NUMERIC column never crashes — GX's failing-sample/observed-value payload only carries raw `Decimal` values when the check actually fails and rows are captured. So this only fires exactly when a warehouse check does its job and catches something real, and the entire run's results (not just that one check) are lost silently — no persisted row at all.

## Repro (verified live, Snowflake `RETAIL.ORDERS_HEADER`)

- `subtotal` (NUMERIC) range check, bound to guarantee 100% pass → succeeds, `n_results=1`.
- Same check, bound to guarantee 100% fail → crashes with the exact `Decimal` `TypeError`, reproduced twice independently.
- `channel` in-set FAIL (string column, not Decimal) → succeeds normally, confirming the bug is Decimal-specific, not FAIL-status-generic.

## Status: pre-existing, currently live in prod

Confirmed `backend/app/core/jsonsafe.py` at prod's deployed commit (`7018d772`) already lacks the `Decimal` branch — this predates the current release delta, it isn't a regression from recent work.

## Impact

Any Snowflake/UC suite with a range/threshold check on a currency, quantity, or other NUMERIC column that legitimately fails loses its entire run's results — the exact "the check caught something" case a DQ platform exists to preserve.

## Fix direction

Add a `decimal.Decimal` branch to `sanitize_json` (`backend/app/core/jsonsafe.py`), mirroring the existing numpy/pandas coercion pattern — e.g. `if isinstance(value, decimal.Decimal): return float(value)`.
EOF
)" \
  --label bug --milestone "v1.1 Week 6 — scale-aware execution + hardening + cycle close" 2>&1

1	"""Make values safe to persist into PostgreSQL ``JSONB`` columns.
2	
3	Great Expectations reports non-finite floats (``NaN``, ``Infinity``) inside
4	result payloads — e.g. a ``partial_unexpected_list`` of failing values, or an
5	``unexpected_percent`` on an empty batch. Python's ``json`` renders these as the
6	bare tokens ``NaN`` / ``Infinity``, which are not valid JSON and which Postgres
7	``JSONB`` rejects. ``sanitize_json`` walks a structure and replaces every
8	non-finite float with ``None`` — and coerces numpy scalars to native Python — so
9	GX results round-trip cleanly into the ``results`` table.
10	
11	Most GX 1.17 results are native Python scalars, but the pandas (flat-file / Unity
12	Catalog) execution engine returns **numpy** scalars in some payloads — notably the
13	``unexpected_index_list`` identifier rows (#415), whose ``numpy.int64`` values are
14	not JSON-serializable and would fail the JSONB insert. ``.item()`` coerces any numpy
15	scalar to its Python equivalent before the finite-float check.
16	"""
17	
18	from __future__ import annotations
19	
20	import math
21	from typing import Any
22	
23	
24	def sanitize_json(value: Any) -> Any:
25	    """Recursively coerce numpy scalars to native Python and replace non-finite
26	    floats with ``None``; leave the rest intact.
27	
28	    Containers are rebuilt (dicts/lists); tuples become lists so the result is
29	    JSON-native. Scalars other than numpy/non-finite-float pass through unchanged.
30	    """
31	    # A numpy scalar (int64/float64/bool_/…) — duck-typed by `item`+`dtype` so `core`
32	    # takes no numpy import (matching profile_service._to_native, and keeping the slim
33	    # typecheck env clean). `.item()` yields the Python equivalent; a numpy float then
34	    # flows into the finite check below.
35	    if hasattr(value, "item") and hasattr(value, "dtype"):
36	        value = value.item()
37	    # pandas' missing-value sentinels: Arrow-backed frames (the iceberg native read,

1	"""Make values safe to persist into PostgreSQL ``JSONB`` columns.
2	
3	Great Expectations reports non-finite floats (``NaN``, ``Infinity``) inside
4	result payloads — e.g. a ``partial_unexpected_list`` of failing values, or an
5	``unexpected_percent`` on an empty batch. Python's ``json`` renders these as the
6	bare tokens ``NaN`` / ``Infinity``, which are not valid JSON and which Postgres
7	``JSONB`` rejects. ``sanitize_json`` walks a structure and replaces every
8	non-finite float with ``None`` — and coerces numpy scalars to native Python — so
9	GX results round-trip cleanly into the ``results`` table.
10	
11	Most GX 1.17 results are native Python scalars, but the pandas (flat-file / Unity
12	Catalog) execution engine returns **numpy** scalars in some payloads — notably the
13	``unexpected_index_list`` identifier rows (#415), whose ``numpy.int64`` values are
14	not JSON-serializable and would fail the JSONB insert. ``.item()`` coerces any numpy
15	scalar to its Python equivalent before the finite-float check.
16	
17	The warehouse (SQLAlchemy/Snowflake) execution engine returns ``decimal.Decimal``
18	for NUMERIC columns. A *passing* check never surfaces one (the failing-sample list
19	is empty), so this only fires when a range/threshold check on a NUMERIC column
20	genuinely fails — the observed-value/failing-sample payload then carries the raw
21	column values, and an unhandled ``Decimal`` crashes the whole result's JSONB insert
22	(#1273), silently discarding the run's results.
23	"""
24	
25	from __future__ import annotations
26	
27	import decimal
28	import math
29	from typing import Any
30	
31	
32	def sanitize_json(value: Any) -> Any:
33	    """Recursively coerce numpy scalars to native Python and replace non-finite
34	    floats with ``None``; leave the rest intact.
35	
36	    Containers are rebuilt (dicts/lists); tuples become lists so the result is
37	    JSON-native. Scalars other than numpy/non-finite-float pass through unchanged.
38	    """
39	    # A numpy scalar (int64/float64/bool_/…) — duck-typed by `item`+`dtype` so `core`
40	    # takes no numpy import (matching profile_service._to_native, and keeping the slim
41	    # typecheck env clean). `.item()` yields the Python equivalent; a numpy float then
42	    # flows into the finite check below.
43	    if hasattr(value, "item") and hasattr(value, "dtype"):
44	        value = value.item()
45	    # pandas' missing-value sentinels: Arrow-backed frames (the iceberg native read,
46	    # #716) surface null cells to GX payloads as `pd.NA` / `pd.NaT`, neither of which
47	    # is JSON-serializable (#751). Duck-typed by type name — same no-pandas-import
48	    # stance as the numpy branch above; both are singletons of these exact types.
49	    # MUST precede the isoformat branch: NaT has .isoformat() but must become null.
50	    if type(value).__name__ in ("NAType", "NaTType"):
51	        return None
52	    # Dates/datetimes: GX coerces between-style kwargs to `datetime.date` in
53	    # `expected_value`, and Arrow-backed frames yield `pd.Timestamp` sample values —
54	    # JSON has no native form for either. `.isoformat()` mirrors
55	    # profile_service._to_native (found live in the #751 review).
56	    if hasattr(value, "isoformat"):
57	        return value.isoformat()
58	    if isinstance(value, decimal.Decimal):
59	        value = float(value)
60	    if isinstance(value, float):
61	        return value if math.isfinite(value) else None
62	    if isinstance(value, dict):
63	        return {key: sanitize_json(item) for key, item in value.items()}
64	    if isinstance(value, (list, tuple)):
65	        return [sanitize_json(item) for item in value]
66	    return value

# dbt Core lineage project (`dataq_lineage`) — harness #609

Self-hosted **dbt Core** project that builds multi-hop lineage objects on top of the
Flow-A retail base tables in Snowflake:

```
DATAQ_DB.RETAIL.{ORDERS_HEADER, ORDER_LINES, CUSTOMERS, PRODUCTS}   ← base (Airflow/ADF loads)
        │  (source)
        ▼
DATAQ_DB.ANALYTICS_STG.{stg_orders, stg_order_lines, stg_customers, stg_products}   ← staging VIEWS
        │  (ref)
        ▼
DATAQ_DB.ANALYTICS.{mart_order_revenue, mart_customer_orders}   ← mart DYNAMIC TABLES (target_lag 1h)
```

It exists to (a) exercise **dbt as a third orchestration layer** (the DataQ-side
provider is a separate issue, #611) and (b) be the **test bed for the G-d lineage
work** (#596 — `manifest.json` is the node-graph input). Harness-only, ADR 0021 —
**not** DataQ app code, **not** git-tracked.

## Why this shape
- **Staging = views, marts = dynamic tables** → real base→staging→mart lineage, and
  the dynamic tables' refresh lag gives DataQ a **freshness monitor** to measure.
- **Self-hosted dbt Core**, host-agnostic on purpose: dbt Cloud free has no
  API/scheduler, dbt-on-Snowflake dies with the trial, Databricks-Jobs-dbt couples
  to the Jobs API. A plain container survives the cloud wind-down (#590/#591); the
  provider (#611) observes it purely through **artifacts + webhook**, never a
  host-specific API.

## Authentication & privileges
- **dbt → Snowflake:** password auth, env-var driven (`profiles.yml` is 100%
  `env_var()`, no secret in the file). Same creds the Airflow loader uses.
- **Role = `DATAQ_LOADER`, not `ACCOUNTADMIN`.** dbt owns the two `ANALYTICS*`
  schemas (needs `CREATE SCHEMA ON DATABASE`, granted in `../terraform/snowflake.tf`
  → `loader_create_schema`) and grants `SELECT`/`USAGE` on them to `DATAQ_READER`
  (the on-run-end hooks) so a DataQ suite (running as the least-priv reader) can read
  the marts. Override with `DBT_SNOWFLAKE_ROLE` (defaults to `DATAQ_LOADER`; we use a
  dbt-specific var so `SNOWFLAKE_ROLE=ACCOUNTADMIN` in `secrets.sh` can't re-escalate).
- **Change tracking (dynamic-table prerequisite):** dynamic tables require change
  tracking on their base tables, and `DATAQ_LOADER` can't enable it (doesn't own
  them). `ORDERS_HEADER` + `CUSTOMERS` → `change_tracking = true` in `snowflake.tf`;
  `ORDER_LINES` + `PRODUCTS` (write_pandas-created) → run **`bootstrap_change_tracking.sql`**
  once as `ACCOUNTADMIN`. ⚠️ `write_pandas` overwrite `CREATE OR REPLACE`s the latter
  two and drops the setting — stable during the wind-down (loader stopped), re-run the
  bootstrap if `flow_a_snowflake_load` runs again.
- **dbt → ADLS (artifact upload):** `AZURE_STORAGE_CONNECTION_STRING` (same seam as
  mockdata's `AdlsStore`).

## Hosting (one image, three homes)
| Context | How |
|---|---|
| Dev iteration | local venv/conda: `source ../secrets.sh && dbt build --profiles-dir .` |
| Azure window | ACA Job `dbt-lineage` on `dataq-cae` (`../terraform/dbt_job.tf`) |
| Post-wind-down | `docker compose -f docker-compose.yml run --rm dbt` |

## Run it

### Local (fastest dev loop — hits live Snowflake, not the Azure harness)
```bash
# one-time: change tracking on the write_pandas base tables (as ACCOUNTADMIN)

content.text:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. The Artifact CSP blocks font CDNs, so don't link a webfont URL and risk a silent fallback. Instead inline the face as a @font-face data URI. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states, not two: an explicit choice stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting stamps *nothing* — most viewers see the un-stamped document, where only `prefers-color-scheme` separates light from dark. Structure the CSS token-level for all three: the bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice beats a dark OS; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also wins in the other direction. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block — a color whose only definition sits behind `[data-theme]` never applies in the un-stamped state, and the page renders one theme's text on the other theme's ground. Two more rules keep each theme resolving as a set: the artifact composites over a ground the viewer paints in *its* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token — a transparent body silently borrows the host's ground; and every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never a literal that only works in one theme. Before publishing, scan the stylesheet for any color declared only inside a media or `[data-theme]` block — that is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — then skip the media query and stamps entirely but still paint the background and every color explicitly, so the page holds on either host ground; make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

**Design plan:**
- **Color**: `--ink:#12151b` (deep blue-black ground), `--surface:#1a1f28`, `--border:#2a3140`, `--text:#e9e6dd` (warm parchment-white, ties to "data" paper/ledger feel), `--text-dim:#9198a8`, `--accent:#5fb3ad` (muted teal — data-clarity metaphor, distinct from the usual AI orange/violet), semantic `--pass:#6fbf73`, `--warn:#e0a63e`, `--crit:#e0655c`.
- **Type**: headers in a system serif stack (Iowan Old Style/Palatino/Georgia) for an engineering-ledger authority; body in system sans; metrics/code in ui-monospace with tabular-nums — three roles, no webfont risk.
- **Layout**: a ledger/report structure — verdict banner up top, then a dense two-column findings grid that collapses to one column on narrow viewports, wide tables scroll in their own containers.

This is a memo/report for a technical stakeholder — polished and legible, not editorial. Let me write it.

# DataQ — deployment guide

How DataQ v1 is deployed to Azure. Infrastructure is **in-repo OpenTofu**
(`deploy/terraform/azure/`, applied — [ADR 0024](../docs/adr/0024-app-deployment-infrastructure.md));
the app rolls out via the **`Deploy`** workflow
([.github/workflows/deploy.yml](../.github/workflows/deploy.yml), `workflow_dispatch`).
The stack is **live** — this is the runbook to provision a fresh environment and to
deploy a new image. Related: [ADR 0025](../docs/adr/0025-production-image-pip-slim.md)
(slim+pip image), [ADR 0023](../docs/adr/0023-container-image-registry-ghcr.md) (GHCR).

Azure is **one** deploy target behind the app's seams (ADR 0010/0013) — the
manifests here are infra config, not business logic. No Azure resource names are
hardcoded in app code; they live only as OpenTofu vars + workflow `vars`/`secrets`.

## Before you deploy: production prerequisites

Read this before a production rollout. It's the "what must change, what access you
need, and what your cloud must provide" checklist; the [provisioning runbook](#one-time-provisioning)
below is the how.

### 1. What you must change (never ship the eval/dev defaults)

The prebuilt-image quickstart ([docs/getting-started](../docs/getting-started.md)) boots
into **email-OTP sign-in by default** (#1150) — a bundled Mailpit catcher stands in for
an SMTP relay, uses a passwordless DB, and binds to loopback. Dev-bypass (no
authentication at all) is an **explicit two-variable downgrade**
(`DATAQ_SIGNIN_EMAIL= DATAQ_AUTH_MODE=bypass`), not the default — and leaving
`DATAQ_SIGNIN_EMAIL` unset entirely refuses to start rather than silently picking a
mode for you. A production deployment must flip all of the following. Values live in
[`deploy/.env.app.prod.example`](.env.app.prod.example) (app settings) +
[`deploy/terraform/azure/variables.tf`](terraform/azure/variables.tf) (infra):

| Setting | Eval default | Production |
|---|---|---|
| `AUTH_DEV_BYPASS` | `true` in the compose file, but **inert by default** — email OTP (`DATAQ_SIGNIN_EMAIL`) wins over it in `auth.py` whenever OTP is configured, which it is out of the box (#1150). It only takes effect once you explicitly clear `DATAQ_SIGNIN_EMAIL` (the documented downgrade). | **`false`** — this is the master auth switch; leaving it on means **no authentication at all**. |
| `AZURE_TENANT_ID` / `AZURE_API_CLIENT_ID` / `AZURE_SPA_CLIENT_ID` | empty | your Azure AD tenant + the two app registrations (API + SPA). |
| **Frontend auth config** | `DATAQ_AUTH_MODE=otp` (eval default — compose sets `${DATAQ_AUTH_MODE:-otp}`) | the **same generic image**, reconfigured at **runtime** — `DATAQ_AUTH_MODE=oidc` + `DATAQ_AUTH_AUTHORITY` / `DATAQ_AUTH_CLIENT_ID` / `DATAQ_AUTH_API_SCOPE` (ADR 0028). **No rebuild** — nginx injects `/config.js` from env. See [frontend/Dockerfile](../frontend/Dockerfile). |
| `SECRET_STORE` | `openbao` (local/eval — ADR 0039) | **`azure_key_vault`** + `AZURE_KEY_VAULT_URL` + the managed identity's `AZURE_CLIENT_ID` (#408). |

Defaults are generous; **tighten `RATE_LIMIT_WEBHOOK_PER_MINUTE`** to your orchestrator's real callback cadence. |
| `RATE_LIMIT_WEBHOOK_IP_PER_MINUTE` | `240` | per-IP ceiling across **all** webhook buckets from one IP (#785) — bounds the aggregate a single IP can spend by rotating provider segments; without it, per-provider buckets would multiply the per-IP webhook budget. |
| `RATE_LIMIT_AUTH_PER_MINUTE` | `10` | strict per-IP cap for `/api/v1/auth/*` (OTP mint/verify, #1127) — checked **before** the bearer branch, so a token can't dodge it. This is the per-IP **backstop**; the tight screw is `AUTH_OTP_REQUEST_PER_EMAIL_PER_10MIN` below. **Tuning note (NAT pools):** per-IP buckets fold onto `RATE_LIMIT_IPV4_PREFIX` (default /24), so an entire corporate-NAT or campus egress range shares these 10 requests/minute — a burst of simultaneous sign-ins from one office can lock the pool out for the window. If your users sign in from behind one egress, **raise this** (30–60 is still a meaningful cap) rather than narrowing the global prefix to /32, which would strip NAT-evasion protection from the `webhook` and `unauth` classes too. The per-email counter is what actually bounds abuse per mailbox, and it is unaffected by NAT. |
| `RATE_LIMIT_IP_PER_MINUTE` | `1200` | per-IP ceiling across **all** bearer buckets from one IP — the rotated-token backstop (a client cycling a fresh random `Bearer` per request can't mint unlimited fresh per-token buckets to dodge the cap). Applies only to the `default` (bearer) class; the unauth class is already per-IP, the webhook class has its own ceiling above. |
| `RATE_LIMIT_IPV4_PREFIX` / `RATE_LIMIT_IPV6_PREFIX` | `24` / `64` | per-IP buckets key on this address **prefix**, not the full address (#789) — a rotating NAT/proxy pool inside one allocation shares a bucket instead of diluting the cap across sibling /32s. `/32` / `/128` disable grouping; widen or narrow per deployment (a CGNAT-heavy user base may warrant `/32`). |
| `RATE_LIMIT_XFF_TRUSTED_HOPS` | `1` | number of trusted proxies that append `X-Forwarded-For` in your deployment — the real client is the entry that many hops from the right. **`1`** for a single-proxy / compose setup (rightmost); **`3`** for the ACA public-envoy→nginx→internal-envoy chain (set in the IaC stack). A chain shorter than this falls back to the socket peer. |
| `AUTH_EMAIL_SMTP_HOST` / `_PORT` / `_USERNAME` / `_FROM` / `_PASSWORD_SECRET_NAME` | unset | email OTP sign-in (ADR 0032) — the third authenticator, for deployments with **no IdP**. Set all four (port defaults to 587) to enable the mailer; the password resolves from the SecretStore **by name**. Deliberately separate from the `EMAIL_*` alert mailer, so a misconfigured alert channel can never block sign-in. **A partial block refuses to boot**, naming the missing vars. **Verify it actually works** with the admin SMTP pre-flight test (#737) — `POST /api/v1/admin/auth-email/test` as a workspace admin sends a real message to the caller's own address and, on failure, names the exact transport stage that broke (`connect` / `tls` / `auth` / `send`) in the error envelope's `detail.stage` — catches a misconfigured relay at install time instead of at a teammate's first sign-in attempt. **`/mcp` stays mounted in this mode** (#1128) — but with no IdP there is no bearer token to validate, so a **PAT (`dq_live_…`) is the only credential it accepts**: raw JWTs and session cookies are both rejected. Tell MCP users to mint an API key. |
| `AUTH_EMAIL_TLS_MODE` | `starttls` | the OTP mailer's SMTP transport ([#1146](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1146)) — `starttls` (default, unchanged: connect in the clear on 587, then upgrade) / **`implicit`** for a submission relay on **:465** (SMTPS — the socket is TLS from the first byte, so `starttls` would fail against it) / **`none`**, a deliberate PLAINTEXT downgrade for a loopback/same-host relay or a throwaway test rig ONLY — the code and the SMTP password cross the wire unencrypted, and every send logs a loud `otp_smtp_tls_disabled` warning naming it. There is deliberately **no** verify-off/insecure-skip option alongside this: `AUTH_EMAIL_CA_BUNDLE` below covers the legitimate "my relay's cert isn't publicly trusted" case, and weakening certificate verification was rejected as a shortcut around it. |
| `AUTH_EMAIL_CA_BUNDLE` | unset | a PEM path of CA certificate(s) the OTP mailer's SMTP connection trusts **instead of** the system store — for an internal relay signed by a private CA ([#1146](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1146)). Scoped to the mailer's own per-send `SSLContext` only — it never touches the process-wide trust store, which is exactly the footgun this replaces: before this option, the only way to reach a private-CA relay was `SSL_CERT_FILE` on the whole api/worker process, silently reconfiguring every OTHER TLS client too (Key Vault, Snowflake, ADLS, webhooks). A path that doesn't name an existing file **refuses to boot**, naming it — the same fail-at-startup discipline as the mailer block above, not a `FileNotFoundError` on the next sign-in attempt. |
| `ADMIN_EMAIL_PREFLIGHT_PER_10MIN` | `3` | per-**admin** cap on `POST /api/v1/admin/auth-email/test`, 10-minute window ([#1147](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1147)). Every call opens a **real SMTP connection to your relay**, and the endpoint otherwise sits in the generic `RATE_LIMIT_AUTHENTICATED_PER_MINUTE` class (300/min per token) that was sized for ordinary API traffic — a scripted or compromised admin token could burn hundreds of connections a minute and get your **sending account throttled or blocked by the relay**, which takes the real sign-in mailer down with it. Over the cap is a plain `429` (`preflight_rate_limited`, `detail.retry_after_seconds`) — there is no anti-enumeration reason to soften it, the caller is a known admin. Uses the **same counter store** as `AUTH_OTP_REQUEST_PER_EMAIL_PER_10MIN` but a **separate key space**, so the two budgets never consume each other; keyed on a digest of the admin's user id, never their address. Counts **before** the send, so a failed attempt still spends a slot. Fails **open** if the counter store is down. **`0` disables the cap** — the endpoint falls back to the 300/min class, re-accepting the #1147 risk in full. |
| `AUTH_OTP_ALLOWED_EMAILS` / `AUTH_OTP_ALLOWED_DOMAINS` | unset | **mandatory** signup allowlist — there is no open registration (DataQ holds failing-row samples, which are PII). At least one entry is required whenever the mailer block is set, or the app refuses to boot. Bootstrap: put your own address in this list **and** `WORKSPACE_ADMIN_EMAILS`. |
| `AUTH_SESSION_TTL_HOURS` | `24` | session cookie lifetime — a fixed horizon with **no refresh token**; re-running the OTP flow is the refresh. Expiry and logout revocation are enforced on every request. |
| `AUTH_SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE` | unset (inferred) | when unset, `Secure` is inferred from `X-Forwarded-Proto` — only trustworthy if the proxy forwards the **real** client-facing scheme. The reference frontend nginx now does: it forwards the **edge's** header and falls back to its own `$scheme` only when there is none (direct connection) — [#1138](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1138); before that fix it overwrote the header with its own plaintext upstream scheme and the cookie shipped **without** `Secure` over HTTPS. Behind your **own** proxy, verify the forwarding — or set this to `true` explicitly, which is valid belt-and-braces on any HTTPS deployment and stops consulting the header at all. Leave unset only for genuinely plain-HTTP local dev — hard-coding `true` there breaks the cookie *silently* (the browser accepts the `Set-Cookie` and then never sends it back). **Runbook note:** the fix rides the **frontend image**, so an existing deployment picks it up on the next frontend roll; until then, or to be certain, set `AUTH_SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE=true` on the api Container App. |
| `AUTH_OTP_REQUEST_PER_EMAIL_PER_10MIN` | `3` | per-**mailbox** cap on code requests, 10-minute window (#1127). **Active regardless of `RATE_LIMIT_ENABLED`** — dev and E2E disable the middleware, and a mail-bomb control a test harness switches off is not a control. Fails **open** if Redis is down (logged once, never the address). A throttled request returns the same uniform `ok` as a successful one; a 429 would tell an attacker which addresses are allow-listed. |
| `AUTH_OTP_REQUEST_MIN_SECONDS` | `1.0` | constant-time **floor** on `POST /api/v1/auth/otp/request` ([#1137](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1137)) — every uniform response (sent / ineligible / throttled) is held to this minimum, so the code-mint + SMTP round trip an eligible address pays no longer stands out against an ineligible one's in-memory lookup. Error responses (502/503) are deliberately **not** padded — they are already non-uniform by design (a mail outage is operator-visible, not a per-address secret). Raise it if your relay is routinely slower than a second; **`0` disables the floor — re-opens the #1137 timing channel**. Not a constant-time guarantee: a send slower than the floor still overruns it, bounded by `AUTH_EMAIL_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`. |
| `AUTH_OTP_VERIFY_MIN_SECONDS` | `0.5` | the same **floor** on `POST /api/v1/auth/otp/verify` ([#1141](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1141)). Every rejected code answers a byte-identical 401, but an address with a **live code outstanding** pays an `UPDATE … RETURNING` + commit that an address with none never pays — and that difference is cheap to set up, because a code is minted **only for an allow-listed address**, so one `otp/request` against the address being probed (uniform `ok` either way, revealing nothing itself) creates it for the price of a per-email quota slot. Every 401 is held to this minimum. A **successful** verification is deliberately **not** padded (a 200 already separates itself, to a caller who by definition knows the code), so real sign-ins stay snappy; neither is the 503 for an unconfigured deployment. Half the request-side floor because there is no SMTP tail to clear — only two DB round trips. **`0` disables it — re-opens the #1141 timing channel.** Same caveat: a DB round trip slower than the floor overruns it. |
| **Frontend OTP mode** | `DATAQ_AUTH_MODE=otp` (already the eval default, #1150) | set `DATAQ_AUTH_MODE=otp` **together with** the backend block above — these are **two coordinated selectors** (ADR 0032 decision 2) and neither can infer the other. Backend OTP on + frontend on `oidc` ⇒ the SPA shows an OIDC flow against an IdP that is not configured; frontend `otp` + backend off ⇒ the code form 503s. |
| `COMPARISON_MAX_ROWS` | `100000` | default per-side row cap for `comparison` checks (ADR 0015) — both sides materialize in worker memory for the diff, so this is a memory guardrail; over-cap runs **fail fast** (never a silently truncated diff). A check's `config.max_rows` overrides it. |
| `APPLICATIONINSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING` | unset | Azure Monitor / App Insights backend for spans + logs (observability, OTel — ADR 0010). |
| `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` | unset | generic OTLP/HTTP backend for spans + logs (#589) — any OTLP consumer (Tempo/Jaeger/Datadog/Collector); set alongside App Insights for parity, or alone for a non-Azure deploy. |
| `OPENLINEAGE_URL` | unset | OpenLineage emission (ADR 0034, #758) — **dark by default**: unset ⇒ zero emission. Point at an OL receiver (Marquez, DataHub's OL endpoint) and every suite run emits START + terminal RunEvents with DQ facets (5s emit timeout, fail-open, no sample rows ever). Advanced transports via the library-owned `OPENLINEAGE__TRANSPORT__*` / `OPENLINEAGE_CONFIG`; `OPENLINEAGE_DISABLED=true` forces dark. |
| `WAREHOUSE_LINEAGE_ENABLED` | unset (`false`) | **`true`** on the **worker only** to run the daily `refresh_warehouse_lineage` sweep (ADR 0034, #858) — **dark by default** because the Snowflake `ACCOUNT_USAGE` / UC `system.access` views it reads need a grant the connection principal may not hold. Set in `containerapps.tf` (`local.worker_env`). Only the worker runs beat, so setting it on the api does nothing. |
| `LINEAGE_PROVIDER` / `MARQUEZ_URL` | unset | **leave unset** unless you run a lineage server. This deployment deliberately does **not** set them (#1086): Marquez is a dev-only compose profile and production is expected to bring its own catalog (ADR 0034). Set them only when pointing at a reachable OL-compatible server. Two failure shapes differ: an unreachable `MARQUEZ_URL` leaves the pull *configured but failing* (fail-soft, logged, pruning deliberately skipped for cross-source safety); **un-setting the provider is now handled** ([#1090](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1090)) — the next daily `refresh_lineage_pull` tick sweeps the orphaned `source='marquez'` edges (logged as `lineage_pull_orphans_purged`; re-configuring re-pulls). A configured-but-broken provider (typo'd name, missing URL) deliberately does NOT purge. |
| `LINEAGE_STALE_AFTER_HOURS` | `48` | staleness window for the asset-view lineage-source banner (#1091): a warehouse lineage source last refreshed longer ago than this is flagged **stale**, independent of error/degraded — a refresh loop that silently stops must not render as healthy. `0` disables. |
| `WAREHOUSE_LINEAGE_MAX_SEEDS` | `500` | seed cap for the Snowflake `GET_LINEAGE` per-seed traversal (#892) — the Enterprise-only top tier walks this many enumerated tables (ADR 0040 seam) per refresh, **two round trips each** (upstream + downstream), so it is a latency/cost bound. Overflow walks the first N in catalog order and logs `get_lineage_seeds_truncated`; `<=0` removes the bound. Ignored on Standard accounts (the tier is edition-gated) and by every other tier. |
| `ASSET_INVENTORY_MAX_TABLES` | `2000` | per-connection cap on the #919 warehouse inventory sync (ADR 0040 — opt-in per connection via the `inventory_sync` config toggle); overflow syncs the first N in catalog order and logs `inventory_sync_truncated`. `<=0` removes the bound. UC connections need `SELECT` on `system.information_schema` (same grant class as the lineage pull's `system.access`). A failing sync is now **visible in the product**, not only in the worker log (#1104): the outcome is stamped on the connection (`inventory_sync_last_attempted_at` / `_last_error` / `_failing_since`) and the connections list shows an "inventory sync failing" badge with a classified reason — the grant-specific wording only when the enumeration query itself was rejected. `inventory_sync_connection_failed` still logs per tick for operators. |
| `POLL_STALENESS_ALERT_AFTER_S` | `1800` | workspace-wide dead-poll alert (#1052), **api-side**: the API lifespan loop alerts the workspace Teams/Slack/email channels when `max(last_polled_at)` over ALL orchestration connections exceeds this age — it fires precisely when the worker is too broken to alert for itself. `0` disables the loop. Set on the **api** (the worker value is ignored — deliberately: the check must not live in the process it monitors). |
| `key_vault_purge_protection` (OpenTofu var) | `false` (bring-up) | **`true`** for a hardened vault (irreversible). |
| Interactive API docs | served | **404 in prod** via the prod-docs gate (`ENVIRONMENT=prod`). |

### 2. Access you need

- **Azure subscription** — rights to create the resource group, Container Apps
  environment, PostgreSQL Flexible Server, Cache for Redis, Key Vault, and Application
  Insights + Log Analytics (Contributor on the RG/subscription); the frontend is a
  Container App too (no Static Web App since ADR 0028). **Plus** `User Access
  Administrator`/`Owner` to grant the managed identity a **custom get+list+set Key Vault
  role** (an RBAC role assignment — read+write so the app can persist/rotate connection
  credentials at runtime, but not the broader built-in Secrets Officer; #622).
- **Azure AD (Entra ID)** — `Application Administrator` (or Global Admin) to create the
  **two app registrations** (API + SPA) and **grant admin consent** for the API scope.
- **Subscription resource-provider registration** — the app's OpenTofu stack registers
  `Microsoft.App`, `Microsoft.Cache`, `Microsoft.KeyVault`, `Microsoft.Web` (see
  [rp.tf](terraform/azure/rp.tf)); the PostgreSQL + monitoring providers
  (`Microsoft.DBforPostgreSQL`, `Microsoft.Insights`, `Microsoft.OperationalInsights`)
  come registered with the shared harness resources (ADR 0024). Registration needs
  subscription-level rights.
- **GitHub repo admin** — to set the Actions [secrets/vars](#github-config-the-workflow-reads)
  and create the OIDC **federated credential** (subject = the repo's `production`
  environment). The GHCR image push uses the built-in `GITHUB_TOKEN` (`packages: write`);
  the package must be **public** so Container Apps pulls it anonymously (ADR 0023).
- **Tooling** — **OpenTofu** (`tofu`; `brew install opentofu`) + the `az` CLI,
  authenticated to the subscription. Not Terraform — ADR 0024 amendment (2026-07-27).

### 3. Cloud prerequisites

DataQ is provider-agnostic by design — Azure is one target behind the app's seams

The swap is **convention, not enforcement** — nothing is OpenTofu-exclusive yet, which is what keeps it reversible; the `encryption {}` follow-up is the one-way door and is deliberately separate. **Unplanned, shipped 2026-07-27 — S3-compatible endpoints (#1063/#1065):** optional `endpoint_url` + `addressing_style` on the `s3` datasource **and** the `dbt` provider, via one shared `core/s3_endpoint.py`; unlocks MinIO / Ceph / R2 / Wasabi / Backblaze. `auto` → **path** addressing when an endpoint is set is load-bearing (MinIO serves the bucket in the path only, so boto3's virtual-host default fails every read), and `endpoint_url` rejects an embedded credential per the #754/#826 rule. **Live-proven against MinIO** — suite 4/4 over 643 real rows, arrival-time freshness read off `LastModified` — because a non-AWS server is a different implementation and those values cross a driver boundary. The dimension backfill (#952) classified **all 30 real prod checks, zero unclassified**, and real asset scorecards show genuine signal. **Live testing found a bug three green suites could not: UC freshness had NEVER worked** (#953) — the Databricks connector returns a TIMESTAMP's MAX as a **str** and the age math accepted only datetime/date, so a datasource the feature matrix marks ✅ produced no reading since #426.
